e: The population of Rome

No census figure for the population of Rome survives. Ancient sources count only certain groups, mainly the adult male citizens entitled to free grain or cash gifts. Modern scholars estimate the total population from these and other indirect evidence, so the figures below are estimates, not data. Even for the same period they differ by as much as a factor of two.

The points are deliberately not joined by a line: there are no data for the years between the estimates, and a curve would invent them. The two largest uncertainties: how large the city was in the middle Republic, and how fast it shrank in the 5th–6th centuries.

Why do the estimates differ?

The grain-dole multiplier. The number of recipients (c. 200,000 under Augustus) counts only adult male citizens. For the total population one must add women, children, slaves, non-citizen foreigners, soldiers and the elite. There is no ancient figure for their share, so the choice of multiplier alone produces differences of hundreds of thousands. This is the route to the often-quoted figure of about one million.

Density. According to Storey (1997), one million inhabitants on the 13.86 km² of the ancient city would mean 72,150 people per square kilometre, similar to the densest parts of modern Hong Kong. The density of the excavated blocks of Pompeii and Ostia gives a much smaller population, about 450,000.

The number of buildings. The 4th-century regionary catalogue lists 46,602 apartment blocks (insulae) and 1,790 houses (domus) (see “The 14 regions in numbers”). If insula means a whole building, this points to a large population; if only a flat or a plot unit, a much smaller one. The meaning of the word is disputed, so no population can be calculated from the figure.

Late antiquity. The spread between estimates is largest for the sieges of the 5th century (410, 455, 472) and the Gothic War of the 6th: scholars interpret the same few pieces of evidence (the recipients of the meat and bread distribution, Procopius’s account) in different ways.
